lines.text: Why do companies rent expensive humanoid robots instead of buying them?
Humanoid robots are two-legged machines built for human spaces.
Companies rent them through Robotics as a Service, or RaaS.
RaaS is a subscription model for leasing robotic labor.
First, companies avoid paying huge cash outlays upfront.
Purchasing hardware locks up capital in depreciating assets.
Renting converts robotic labor into an operating expense.
Businesses get cutting-edge physical AI without long commitments.
Second, renting dodges rapid hardware obsolescence.
Humanoid designs keep upgrading.
A purchased robot quickly becomes outdated technology.
Under rental contracts, vendors swap old models for new ones.
In June 2024, GXO deployed Digit humanoids in Flowery Branch, Georgia.
Those rented bipedal robots moved over 100,000 totes across live operations.
In October 2026, GXO announced rentals in North Carolina and Tennessee.
Those deployments start in early 2027.
Some think humanoids are already cheaper than workers and fully autonomous.
In 2026, GXO's CEO said zero warehouse humanoids would reach production.
Companies rent humanoids because financial payback at scale remains unproven.
Renting lets firms test automation while shifting maintenance risks to vendors.
Would you rent or buy a robot to do your job?
